plain_title: When weed stops being a choice
one_liner: A pattern of cannabis use that a person can't control and keeps up despite harm, often with withdrawal when stopping.
in_simple_words: Cannabis is widely used and often seen as harmless, but some people develop a use disorder: using more than planned, failing to cut down, craving, needing it to feel normal, and continuing despite problems with motivation, memory, mood, money, or relationships. Withdrawal is real: irritability, poor sleep, anxiety, and low appetite for a week or two. Today's cannabis is often far stronger than in the past, and heavy use in the teens carries extra risks. It is treatable.
what_it_can_feel_like: Everyone said you can't get addicted to weed. Then I tried to stop and couldn't sleep or eat for ten days.
I wasn't 'wasting my life'. I just couldn't do anything without smoking first, and that scared me.
r/leaves got me through the first month. Strangers who'd done it.
common_signs: Using more or more often than intended
Trying to cut down and not managing
Needing cannabis to sleep, eat, relax, or feel normal
Irritability, insomnia, anxiety, or low appetite when stopping
Lost motivation, memory problems, or falling behind at school or work
Continuing despite problems with mood, money, or relationships

myths_vs_facts.fact: Around 1 in 10 people who use cannabis develop a use disorder, and more among those who start young or use daily. Withdrawal is real.
Modern high-THC products are potent. Heavy use, especially in the teens, raises the risk of psychosis, anxiety, and lasting effects on learning.

myths_vs_facts.myth: If it's legal, it can't be a problem.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Legal status says nothing about whether use has become hard to control.

how_common.plain: Cannabis is the most widely used illicit drug in the US, with over 1 in 5 people using it in the past year. A significant minority of users develop a use disorder; exact figures to be confirmed.
how_common.figure: 21.8% of people aged 12+ used cannabis in the past year (NSDUH 2023); cannabis use disorder prevalence to be confirmed from the same release
how_common.note: The 2023 NSDUH cannabis use disorder figure was not confirmed in this session.

what_helps.plain_summary: Talking therapies are the main treatment: CBT, motivational enhancement therapy, and contingency management (rewards for staying off), often combined. Brief interventions help people who want to cut down. There is no approved medication for cannabis use disorder itself, though a doctor may treat sleep or mood problems during withdrawal. Peer support online and in groups helps many people through the early weeks.
evidence_based_options: Treatment of co-occurring anxiety, depression, or psychosis
self_help_that_supports_care: Planning for the first two weeks: sleep will be rough, then it improves
Removing paraphernalia and changing routines around use
Exercise, which helps withdrawal sleep and mood

when_to_reach_out: If you've tried to cut down and can't, need cannabis to function, or it's affecting school, work, mood, or motivation, talk to a doctor, a drug helpline, or a therapist. Seek help urgently if you experience paranoia, hearing voices, or confusion.
is_not: Occasional use without loss of control or harm isn't a disorder. Medical cannabis taken as prescribed isn't a use disorder, though dependence can still develop.
hope_note: Most people who quit cannabis find the fog lifting within weeks and wonder why they waited.

content_notes: No dosing, sourcing, or 'how to use' detail. Harm-reduction pointers only to official organizations.
Crisis strip with substance helplines required.

in_young_people: Teenage brains are more vulnerable to cannabis. Heavy use before age 18 is linked to a higher risk of use disorder, poorer school outcomes, and psychosis in those at risk. Family-based treatments work well for teens.
across_cultures: Cannabis is legal, decriminalized, or strictly prohibited depending on country, which shapes stigma and access to help. In some cultures it has traditional or religious uses; the DSM's concern is loss of control and harm, not use itself.

sub_sections.title: Cannabis intoxication and withdrawal
sub_sections.text: Intoxication can include anxiety, paranoia, and, with high doses, brief psychotic symptoms. Withdrawal peaks in the first week and mostly resolves within two.

sub_sections.title: Cannabis-induced psychosis
sub_sections.text: Heavy use can trigger psychotic symptoms, usually resolving with abstinence, but raising the risk of a lasting psychotic disorder in some people.
